prompt: Building `cmd/go` took 21.332 seconds from an empty cache and 0.837 seconds straight after. What made the second build fast?

choices.text: The output went to `/dev/null`, so nothing had to be linked
choices.why: Both builds wrote to `/dev/null`; that only throws the result away, and the first one was slow all the same.

choices.text: Every one of the 334 packages was already compiled, waiting in the build cache
choices.why: Right. `go clean -cache` had emptied it before the first build; the second found all 334 packages compiled.

choices.text: The second build used all four processors and the first used one
choices.why: The first build is the one whose `user` time, 57 seconds, shows several processors busy at once.

choices.text: Go only compiles the source files edited since the previous build
choices.why: The unit the cache keeps is a compiled package, not an edited file, and nothing was edited between the two runs.

prompt: On the lab's x86-64 machine you run `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build` on the program `why` and copy the result to a 64-bit ARM Linux server. What does it print there?

choices.text: `compiled for linux/amd64`, since that is the machine that compiled it
choices.why: `runtime.GOOS` and `runtime.GOARCH` name the target of the build, and the target was arm64.

choices.text: Nothing: `Exec format error`, as in the lab
choices.why: The lab refused it because the lab is x86-64. An ARM server is the machine the binary was built for.

choices.text: `compiled for linux/arm64`
choices.why: Right. The two values are fixed at compile time and report the system the binary was built for, wherever it runs.

choices.text: An error about the missing Go installation on the server
choices.why: A Go binary carries its runtime inside it; nothing of Go has to be installed where it runs.

prompt: A colleague runs `file` on a Go binary and reads `dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`. Going by lesson 1, which of these can explain it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The program uses `net`, which keeps a route through the C library
choices.why: Yes. `lookup` imported `net` and came out needing `libc.so.6`.

choices.text: It was a native build on a machine with a C compiler on the `PATH`
choices.why: Yes. That is when `go doc cmd/cgo` says cgo is enabled, and the lab had `gcc`.

choices.text: It was built with `CGO_ENABLED=0`
choices.why: That is the fix, not the cause: the same `lookup` built with it came out `statically linked`.

choices.text: Every Go binary links the Go runtime as a shared library
choices.why: The runtime is inside the file; `why` carried it and `ldd` found no shared library at all.

prompt: Suppose go1.28.0 comes out in February 2027, on the calendar lesson 2 describes. Which versions then receive fix releases?

choices.text: 1.26, 1.27 and 1.28, the last three
choices.why: Three would mean support until three newer releases exist; the rule says two.

choices.text: Only 1.27 and 1.28
choices.why: Right. Once 1.28 exists, 1.26 has two newer releases and stops, as 1.25 did when 1.27 arrived.

choices.text: Only 1.28, the newest
choices.why: On 18 August 2026 fix releases came out for 1.25 and 1.26 alongside 1.27.0, so more than the newest is looked after.

choices.text: Every version since Go 1, because of the compatibility promise
choices.why: The promise is about source code compiling on new releases, not about fixing old ones forever.

prompt: A blog post tells you to move your project, which has its own `go.mod`, from `~/projects/api` into `~/go/src` or it will not build. What is true?

choices.text: It is needed so that the go command can find the project's imports
choices.why: That was GOPATH mode, the legacy behaviour `go help gopath` describes; it is not what a module uses.

choices.text: The advice is out of date: a module builds wherever it sits
choices.why: Right. A directory with a `go.mod` at its root says what its code is called, which is why `~/hello` built in lesson 4.

choices.text: It is only needed for `go install`, which writes into `GOPATH`
choices.why: `go install` puts the binary in `~/go/bin`; where the source sits does not matter to it, as lesson 4 showed from `~/hello`.

choices.text: It is true, because `~/go/src` is where `GOMODCACHE` points
choices.why: `GOMODCACHE` is `~/go/pkg/mod`, read-only downloads; and today `~/go` has no `src` at all.

prompt: `go env ___` lists every setting that differs from the defaults, wherever it came from; in the lab it printed only `GOTOOLCHAIN='local'`.
In the directory `~/work`, a `go.mod` says `module example.com/tools/report`. What file does `go build` leave there?

choices.text: `work`, after the directory
choices.why: The directory's name plays no part; it is the module path that names the binary.

choices.text: `main`, after the package that builds into a program
choices.why: Every program's package is `main`, so that name would tell no two programs apart.

choices.text: `report`, after the last element of that path
choices.why: Right. `go build` names the binary after the last element of the module path, as `hello` was named.

choices.text: Nothing: the binary stays in the build cache
choices.why: That is `go run`. `go build` leaves the binary next to the source.

prompt: A function declares `total := 0` and never uses `total`. Of the compiler, `gofmt` and `go vet`, what happens?

choices.text: The compiler refuses to build it at all: `declared and not used: total`
choices.why: Right. A local variable declared and never used is refused like an unused import.

choices.text: It builds, and `go vet` reports the variable
choices.why: `go vet` is for what is valid Go and nearly always a bug; this is not valid Go, so it never gets that far.

choices.text: `gofmt` deletes the line when it lays out the file
choices.why: `gofmt` changes layout only: spaces, tabs, blank lines. It never removes a statement.

choices.text: Nothing: an unused variable is legal and costs nothing
choices.why: Go makes it an error on purpose, because an unused variable is often a typo for one that is used.

prompt: Which of these are true of `go run .`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It compiles the program to a binary before running it
choices.why: Yes. Go has no interpreter; `go run` compiles and then runs the binary.

choices.text: It keeps the binary in the build cache
choices.why: Yes, which is why the second run took 44 milliseconds.

choices.text: It reads the source and runs it line by line, like an interpreter
choices.why: It looks like that and is not: the first run spent four seconds compiling.

choices.text: It leaves the binary in the current directory, next to `go.mod`
choices.why: That is `go build`. After `go run` there is no file you can find.

prompt: A package declares `const answer int = 42`, and `main` says `var exact float64 = answer`. What happens?

choices.text: It compiles, because 42 fits in a `float64`
choices.why: Fitting is the test for an untyped constant. This one was given the type `int`, and the type is what is checked.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to use an `int` constant as a `float64` value
choices.why: Right. Like the `int8` case: a typed constant keeps its type, and Go does not turn one numeric type into another by itself.

choices.text: It compiles, and `exact` holds 42.0 converted at run time
choices.why: Go never converts on your behalf, at compile time or at run time.

choices.text: It compiles only if `exact` is declared with `:=` instead
choices.why: `exact := answer` would compile, and give `exact` the type `int`, so it would not be a `float64` at all.

prompt: Inside one function: `x, err := first()` and, two lines below in the same block, `x, err := second()`. What does the compiler say?

choices.text: Nothing: `:=` with two names assigns whichever already exist
choices.why: That holds when at least one name on the left is new. Here both already exist.

choices.text: `declared and not used: x`, because the first `x` was replaced before being read
choices.why: Whether `x` is read is a separate question; the second line is refused before that matters.

choices.text: `no new variables on left side of :=`
choices.why: Right. `:=` with several names needs at least one of them new; the fix is `x, err = second()`.

choices.text: Nothing: the second line declares a new `x` and a new `err` that shadow the first
choices.why: Shadowing needs an inner block. In the same block a name cannot be declared twice.

prompt: A package-level variable that nothing reads compiles. Inside a function, an unread `count` is refused with: `declared and not ___: count`.
`const ( A = iota * 10; B; C; D )`, one name per line. What is the value of `C`?

`var cfg *Config` is declared at the top of `main`. Inside `if debug { cfg, err := load(); if err != nil { return }; fmt.Println("loaded", cfg.Name) }`, and after the `if`, `run(cfg)`. With `debug` true and `load` succeeding, what does `run` receive?

choices.text: The `*Config` that `load` returned
choices.why: That one went into a second `cfg`, declared by `:=` inside the `if` block and gone at its closing brace.

choices.text: `nil`, the zero value of the outer `cfg`
choices.why: Right. Both names were new to the `if` block, so `:=` declared both, the same shape as the shadowed `err` of `total`.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses the inner `cfg` as declared and not used
choices.why: It would, if nothing read it. The block prints `cfg.Name`, so the inner `cfg` is used, and nothing complains, as `go vet` exited 0 on `total`.

choices.text: Nothing: `:=` cannot redeclare a name that exists outside the block
choices.why: It can, and that is the trouble: an inner block may reuse an outer name and hide it.

prompt: Match each declaration with what `fmt.Printf("%#v", v)` prints for it before anything is assigned.
`var x int16 = 32767`, then `x++`, then `fmt.Println(x)`. What does it print?
Which of these builds, and then wraps around when it runs?

choices.text: `const limit int8 = 127` and then `next := limit + 1`
choices.why: `limit` is a typed constant, so the sum is a constant too, and the compiler refuses it: `overflows int8`.

choices.text: `var v int8 = 127` and then `v = v + 1`
choices.why: Right. `v` is a variable, so nothing is known until run time, and 127 + 1 in an `int8` silently becomes −128.

choices.text: `var small int8 = 128`
choices.why: 128 is a constant the compiler can check, and it refused it with `(overflows)`.

choices.text: `fmt.Println(1 << 100)`, which wraps to 0
choices.why: An untyped constant that has to become an `int` and does not fit is a compile error, never a wrapped value.

prompt: Put these types in order of the largest value each can hold, smallest first.
`s` is a string that may be empty. What does `if len(s) > 0 && s[0] == '#' {` do when `s` is `""`?

choices.text: It panics, because `s[0]` does not exist in an empty string
choices.why: It would if it were evaluated. `&&` found its left side false and never looked at the right one.

choices.text: It does not compile, because `s[0]` is a byte and `'#'` a rune
choices.why: `'#'` is an untyped rune constant, 35, and it fits in a byte, so the comparison compiles.

choices.text: The condition is simply false, and `s[0]` is never evaluated at all
choices.why: Right. Short-circuit evaluation: the length test guards the index, as `people > 0` guarded the division.

choices.text: Both sides are evaluated first, so the answer depends on what `s[0]` holds
choices.why: `&&` stops as soon as the answer is known; in Go the order of the two tests is part of the meaning.

prompt: Plain ASCII takes one byte, `é` two and `€` three. What does `len("a€é")` return?
`count` is an `int`, and `tests` and `lint` are `bool`. Which of these lines does the compiler refuse? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `if count {`
choices.why: Refused: `non-boolean condition in if statement`. No type but `bool` stands where a condition goes.

choices.text: `pair := 'ab'`
choices.why: Refused: `more than one character in rune literal`. Single quotes hold one rune.

choices.text: `odd := tests != lint`
choices.why: Compiles. `!=` between two booleans is Go's exclusive or.

choices.text: `var b byte = 'é'`
choices.why: Compiles, because 233 fits in a byte. That is the trap: the byte holds the code point, not the `c3 a9` of a string.

choices.text: `ready := bool(count)`
choices.why: Refused: `cannot convert count (variable of type int) to type bool`. There is no conversion from a number to a truth value.

choices.text: Joining a first name and a surname once, for a greeting
choices.why: Once, `+` costs nothing worth saving: join a few strings with `+`.

choices.text: Building a report out of 50,000 lines, one on every turn of a loop
choices.why: Right. `+=` in a loop copies everything built so far on every turn, which is how 100,000 rounds took 3.7 seconds.

choices.text: Changing the first letter of a string to upper case in place
choices.why: Nothing changes a string in place; a Builder makes a new string too, and `"H" + s[1:]` is the simple way.

choices.text: Keeping only the first 80 bytes of a large string
choices.why: That is the case for `strings.Clone`, which copies a small substring so the large one can go.

prompt: A raw literal cannot hold a backquote, because the backquote ends it. A string that needs one is written in ___ quotes.
A package has `type Feet float64`, `type Meters float64` and `func ToMeters(f Feet) Meters { return Meters(f) }`. What does `ToMeters(10)` return?

choices.text: It does not compile, since `Feet` cannot become `Meters`
choices.why: Two types with the same underlying type convert into each other; only mixing them without a conversion is refused.

choices.text: 3.048, converted by the type system
choices.why: Nothing in the language knows how feet relate to metres, as nothing knew how Celsius relates to Fahrenheit.

choices.text: 10 metres: the conversion relabelled the number and did no arithmetic

choices.text: 10, after a vet warning about lost precision

`p := [2]int{1, 2}` and `q := []int{1, 2}`. Which of these compile? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `fmt.Println(p == [2]int{1, 2})`
choices.why: Compiles: two arrays of the same type compare element by element.

choices.text: `fmt.Println(q == nil)`
choices.why: Compiles: `nil` is the one thing a slice may be compared to.

choices.text: `fmt.Println(q == []int{1, 2})`
choices.why: Refused: `slice can only be compared to nil`. `slices.Equal` compares the elements.

choices.text: `var r [3]int = p`
choices.why: Refused: the length is part of the type, and a `[2]int` is not a `[3]int`.

prompt: `s := []int{1, 2, 3}`, then `t := s` and `t[0] = 9`. What does `fmt.Println(s)` print?

choices.text: `[1 2 3]`, because assigning copies the elements
choices.why: That is what assigning an array does. A slice copies its three words, and the pointer leads to the same array.
Right. `t` is a second slice over the one array, as the parameter of `setFirst` was.

choices.text: Nothing: `t := s` is refused, since slices cannot be copied
choices.why: Slices can be assigned freely; it is `==` between two of them that is refused.

choices.text: `[9 2 3]` only if `s` was sliced from a named array
choices.why: A slice literal builds an array too; it simply has no name. Sharing works the same way.

prompt: `s == u` between two `[]int` is refused with `invalid operation: s == u (slice can only be compared to ___)`.
`base := []int{1, 2, 3}` has length 3 and capacity 3. Then `a := append(base, 4)` and `b := append(base, 5)`. What does `fmt.Println(a, b)` print?

choices.text: `[1 2 3 5] [1 2 3 5]`, because both appends wrote into one array
choices.why: That was `path`, which had spare capacity. `base` has none, so neither append can write into its array.
Right. With length equal to capacity, each `append` allocates a new array and copies first, so `a` and `b` share nothing.

choices.text: `[1 2 3 4] [1 2 3 4 5]`, since `b` is appended after `a`
choices.why: Both appends start from `base`, which still has length 3; `a` is never their input.

choices.text: It panics on the second append, past the capacity
choices.why: `append` never panics for lack of room; it allocates a bigger array. Only an index or a reslice is checked.

prompt: `s := make([]int, 2, 5)`. Match each line to what happens.

`panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:6] with capacity 5`

prompt: Which line makes an empty slice with room for 100 `int`s, ready to `append` to without allocating again?

choices.text: `s := make([]int, 100)`
choices.why: That is 100 zeros already, not room: an `append` would land at position 100.
Length first, then capacity: with constants the compiler refuses this as `length and capacity swapped`.
Right. Length 0, capacity 100: one array, and `append` never leaves it for the first 100 elements.

choices.text: `var s [100]int`, with `append` writing into it
choices.why: That is an array, with a fixed length, and `append` takes a slice.

prompt: `raw := []byte{192, 168, 0, 10, 0, 80}` holds six bytes. What does `[4]byte(raw)` do?

choices.text: It panics, because the slice is longer than the array
choices.why: Only shorter panics. Longer is fine: the conversion takes what it needs.

choices.text: It copies the first four bytes into a new array; the other two are not read at all
choices.why: Right. That is how `netip.AddrFrom4([4]byte(raw))` printed `192.168.0.10`.

choices.text: It is refused, because the compiler cannot see that `raw` has four bytes
choices.why: The compiler accepts it and leaves the length check to run time, where a short slice panics.

choices.text: It gives an array that shares the slice's first four bytes
choices.why: Sharing is what `(*[4]byte)(raw)`, the pointer conversion, does; the array conversion copies.

pairs.right: `panic: assignment to entry in nil map`

right_distractors: a compile error, since `m` was never made

prompt: A map literal lists `"ana": 31` and, three lines further down, `"ana": 32`. What happens?

choices.text: The map holds 32, the last value written
choices.why: That is what two assignments `ages["ana"] = …` do. In a literal, one value would be thrown away unseen, so it is refused.

choices.text: The map holds 31, and the second pair is ignored
choices.why: Ignoring it silently is exactly what the compiler refuses to do.

choices.text: It panics when the literal is built at run time
choices.why: Both keys are constants written in the source, so the compiler sees the clash before anything runs.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: `duplicate key "ana" in map literal`
choices.why: Right. A key appears once, and a literal naming one twice does not compile.

prompt: A tool writes a settings file by walking a `map[string]string` with `range`. Every run produces a different file from the same settings, and reviewers see diffs nobody made. What fixes it?

choices.text: Building the map with `make(map[string]string, n)` and the right size
choices.why: The size only reserves room; every walk still starts at a random place.

choices.text: Inserting the keys in alphabetical order
choices.why: A map keeps no insertion order; on a small map the order comes out rotated, and on a big one it is shuffled.

choices.text: Taking `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))` and walking that slice
choices.why: Right. The map answers what each value is; the sorted slice of keys answers in what order.

choices.text: Keeping the settings under eight keys so they fit in one group
choices.why: Even then the start is random: four keys gave three different first keys in six runs, and the group is not a promise of the language.

prompt: A `Session` struct has a field `Token string` that other packages must read, and it must never appear in the JSON the service logs. Which declaration does that?

choices.text: ``Token string `json:"-"` ``
choices.why: Right. A tag of `-` keeps the field out always, and the capital T keeps it visible to other packages.

choices.text: `token string`, in lower case, with no tag
choices.why: It would stay out of the JSON, and out of every other package too, which the field needs.

choices.text: ``Token string `json:"token,omitempty"` ``
choices.why: `omitempty` drops the field only while it is empty; a real token would go out.

choices.text: ``Token string `json:"token,omitzero"` ``, which hides any value
choices.why: `omitzero` drops the field when it holds its zero value, and a filled token is not zero.

prompt: Which of these struct tags does `go vet` report? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: ``json: "name"``
choices.why: Reported: the space after the colon makes the whole tag unreadable, `bad syntax for struct tag value`.

choices.text: ``json:"email, omitempty"``
choices.why: Reported: `suspicious space in struct tag value`. The option would be ` omitempty`, which is no option.

choices.text: ``json:"email,omitempty"``
choices.why: Correct as written: a key, a comma and the option, with no space.
A valid tag: it keeps the field out of the JSON always.

prompt: `Person` has a field `Name`; `User` embeds `Person`; `Admin` embeds `User`. Nothing else declares `Name`. For `a` an `Admin`, what does `a.Name` do?

choices.text: It is refused: promotion only reaches one level down
choices.why: The search goes level by level for as far as it has to; there is no limit of one.

choices.text: It reads `a.User.Person.Name`, two levels down
choices.why: Right. `Admin` has no `Name`, nor has `User` at its own level, so the search goes one level further and finds the only one.

choices.text: It is ambiguous, because `User` and `Person` both lead to `Name`
choices.why: Ambiguity needs two fields of one name at the same depth. Here there is one `Name`, reached through a chain.

choices.text: It reads a copy of the name that `Admin` keeps at its own level
choices.why: Promotion copies nothing; `%+v` would show `Name` nested inside `Person` inside `User`.

prompt: In a `go 1.27.1` module, `e := Employee{Person: Person{Name: "Ana"}, Email: "ana@example.com"}`, where `Email` is a field of `Person`. What happens?

choices.text: It compiles, and `Email` is merged into the `Person` given
choices.why: No merging: the two forms would write the same field twice, so they cannot be mixed for one embedded struct.

choices.text: It compiles, and the `Email` written last wins
choices.why: Neither wins; the literal is refused before any value is built.

choices.text: It is refused, because promoted fields cannot be set in a literal
choices.why: Since Go 1.27 they can, as `Employee{Name: "Ana", Email: …, Company: …}` showed; the trouble is mixing the two forms.

choices.text: Refused: `cannot specify promoted field Email and enclosing embedded field Person`
choices.why: Right. Either the whole `Person` or its promoted fields, not both.

prompt: `n := 81`, then `for n > 1 { n /= 3 }`. How many times does the body run?

choices.text: 0, 1, 2 and 3, one per character
choices.why: That would be a count of characters. `range` over a string gives the byte offset where each rune starts.

choices.text: 0 to 5, one per byte
choices.why: That is the three-clause loop over `len(s)`. `range` decodes the UTF-8 and visits each rune once.
Right. The `€` starts at 0 and takes three bytes, so `u` starts at 3, as the `!` after `é` started at 5 in `café`.

choices.text: 0, 1, 2 and 3, plus U+FFFD for the bytes that do not fit

prompt: A `range` over a map adds a new key for each key it visits. What does Go say about the keys added during the loop?

choices.text: Each may be visited or skipped; the specification leaves it open
choices.why: Right. Which is why new entries belong in a second map, copied over when the loop is done.

choices.text: None are visited, because `range` reads a map once, as it reads a slice once
choices.why: Reading once is the slice's rule. For a map, an entry created during the walk can turn up.

choices.text: All are visited, so the loop can never end
choices.why: Nothing promises that they are visited, and nothing promises that they are not.

choices.text: It panics, as changing a map during a walk always does
choices.why: Deleting during a walk is explicitly allowed, and adding does not panic either; it is only unpredictable.

choices.text: Marking happens while the program keeps running

choices.text: Live values are moved together to close the gaps
choices.why: That would be compacting, and Go's collector never moves a value on the heap.

choices.why: The rule is about the package, not the module: a method goes in the package that defines the type.

choices.text: It is refused: `cannot define new methods on non-local type temp.Celsius`
choices.why: Right. As with `time.Duration`, only the package that defines a type may give it methods; `main` can define its own type on top.

choices.text: It compiles, because `Celsius` is a defined type and not an alias

choices.text: It compiles, and `Kelvin` is added to `temp` for every importer
choices.why: Importing a package can never add a method to its types; that is the point of the rule.

prompt: `r.Area` without brackets is a method value of type `func() float64`. `Rect.Area`, named through the type, is a method ___ of type `func(main.Rect) float64`.

choices.why: Right. `c` is a copy of each element; `c.Inc()` takes `&c` and counts that copy. `list[i].Inc()` would reach the elements.

choices.text: `[{1} {1}]`, because a pointer method changes what it is called on

prompt: Type `T` has `func (t T) A()` and `func (t *T) B()`, and `t` is a variable of type `T`. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The method set of `*T` holds both `A` and `B`
choices.why: Yes. From an address the compiler can always reach the value and copy it for `A`.

choices.text: `t.B()` compiles
choices.why: Yes. `t` is a variable, so Go rewrites the call as `(&t).B()`.

choices.text: The method set of `T` holds both `A` and `B`
choices.why: Only `A`. The pointer method needs an address that a value in an interface does not have.

choices.text: `var x interface{ B() } = t` compiles
choices.why: Refused: `T does not implement … (method B has pointer receiver)`. `&t` would compile.

prompt: A `Grid` type holds a `[1000][1000]float64`, and all of its methods only read it. Going by lesson 26's four questions, which receiver should they have?

choices.text: A value receiver, since nothing changes the grid
choices.why: Question 1 alone would allow it; question 3 overrules it, because every call would copy eight million bytes.

choices.text: A pointer on every one of them, since each call would otherwise copy eight million bytes
choices.why: Right. A type that carries a large array takes a pointer, and one kind of receiver per type keeps its method sets whole.

choices.text: Value receivers on small methods and pointers on slow ones
choices.why: The copy is of the receiver, not of the method's work, and mixing kinds leaves the value's method set incomplete.

choices.text: Either: the compiler passes large receivers by pointer anyway
choices.why: Nothing does that; lesson 22 measured 350,746 ns to pass an 8,000,000-byte array by value.

prompt: The build stops with `Disk does not implement Store (wrong type for method Get)`, then `have Get(string) []byte` and `want Get(string) ([]byte, error)`. What is wrong with `Disk`?

choices.text: It has no method called `Get` at all
choices.why: That would read `missing method Get`. `wrong type` means the name is there.

choices.text: It never declared that it implements `Store`
choices.why: Nothing in Go declares that; a type fits by having the methods, and the message is about one of them.

choices.text: Its `Get` has a pointer receiver and a value was passed
choices.why: That case ends in `(method Get has pointer receiver)`, not in a `have` and a `want`.

choices.text: Its `Get` returns only `[]byte`, where `Store` asks for `[]byte` and an `error`
choices.why: Right. `have` is what the type declares and `want` what the interface asks; the results must match in type and order.

prompt: `NewCache()` is declared to return a `Cache` interface listing `Get` and `Set`. The concrete type it builds also has a `Stats()` method. What does a caller of `NewCache` lose?

choices.text: Nothing: the interface holds the concrete value, so `c.Stats()` can still be called
choices.why: Through a `Cache`, the compiler allows only what `Cache` lists; `Stats` is not in it.

choices.text: `Stats`, which it can no longer call without a type assertion
choices.why: Right. The same reason `os.Open` returns an `*os.File`: return the concrete type, and the caller keeps every method.

choices.text: The ability to pass the cache where a `Cache` is asked for
choices.why: That is the one thing it keeps. A concrete result could be passed there too, which is why returning one costs nothing.

choices.text: Speed, since every call through an interface is checked at run time
choices.why: Whether a value fits is checked at compile time, at the point of use; the cost lesson 27 names is the lost methods.

prompt: `{"ids": [1, 2]}` is decoded with `json.Unmarshal` into a `map[string]any`. What does `fmt.Printf("%T", doc["ids"])` print?

choices.text: `[]interface {}`

choices.text: `[]any`, the name the documentation uses
choices.why: The type is that one, but `%T` prints `any` as `interface {}`, its long name.

prompt: `var buf *bytes.Buffer` is never assigned, and then `var w io.Writer = buf`. What does `fmt.Println(w != nil)` print?

choices.text: `false`, because `buf` is nil and `w` holds `buf`

choices.text: `true`

choices.text: Nothing: a nil pointer cannot be assigned to an interface

choices.text: It panics, because comparing reads through the nil pointer

prompt: `j := errors.Join(fmt.Errorf("save: %w", fs.ErrPermission), errors.New("disk full"))`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
